warmup.q: A test starts 2 threads that each call a counter's unsafe hit() method 1,000 times, then checks the total. It passes 20 runs out of 20. What's the most likely reason?
options: The counter is thread-safe after all
The first thread usually finishes before the second one starts, so they never overlap
The JIT compiler fixed the race
JUnit runs threads one at a time
warmup.why: 1,000 increments take microseconds, about as long as starting a thread. The first thread is often done before the second begins, so there's no overlap to go wrong, and the test proves nothing. Make the threads start together with a latch, use more of them, and run far more operations, as the first section shows.

opening:
Picture the refund desk at a shop. A customer who brings something back gets a refund, money paid back, and one sale can be refunded in several parts. The rule: the refunds for one sale must never add up to more than the sale. The shop's program handles refunds on several threads at once. (A thread is one path of work running beside others in one program.) So the team wrote a test: two threads ask for refunds at once, and the total must stay within the sale. It has passed every day for a year.

Then, on the first busy day of a sale, a coat that sold for 100.00 is refunded 160.00. The customer is delighted. The shop is not.

The test wasn't lying. Its two threads never met: on a quiet machine, the first finished before the second started. This lesson turns the track's "run it a few times" into a skill. We'll make test threads collide, swap sleeps for latches, let jcstress search the timings for us, and read what a stuck or slow JVM, the program that runs your Java code, can tell us. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a refund test that passed for a year while a coat went out at 160.00, because its threads never met. A start latch, more threads and many rounds made them collide every time. A latch replaced the sleep, jcstress counted two billion meetings, and a dump and a recording showed what the stuck and slow threads were doing.

Now search your own tests for Thread.sleep(. Each one is a guess about timing. Replace it with a latch, or with polling that has a deadline.

That ends this track. Next, we'll look beneath the threads at memory itself, starting with a loop that never stops: how can one thread miss a write that another thread made long ago?

sections.h: Making test threads collide: the stress test
sections.html:
Let's start with the smallest form of the problem. In Race conditions, a counter's count++ lost updates when two threads ran it at once, because count++ is three steps: read, add, write. Here's the kind of test most people write for it:

Java
// Naive: two threads that may never meet
Counter c = new Counter();
Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); });
Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); });
a.start(); b.start();
a.join(); b.join();
assertThat(c.count).isEqualTo(2_000);
Kotlin
// Naive: two threads that may never meet
val c = Counter()
val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } }
val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } }
a.join(); b.join()
assertThat(c.count).isEqualTo(2_000)

The Try it runs this test twenty times against that racy counter. Then it runs a stress test, which we'll build in a moment, twenty times against the same counter:

naive test  (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed 1 of 20 runs
stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed 20 of 20 runs

Same code, same bug. The naive test caught it once in twenty runs, and in another run here, not at all. Race conditions put it this way: a race is shy around small numbers. A thousand increments take a few microseconds, about as long as starting a thread, so the first thread is often done before the second begins. On a quiet machine, the scheduler, the part of the system that decides which thread runs when, is kind to small tests. It runs them one after the other, and the bug never gets its chance.

A test that doesn't force overlap is really a single-threaded test. Five habits turn it into a stress test, a test that runs code on many threads at once, many times, to make races show up:

  1. Hold every thread at a start line and release them together, with the start latch from Synchronizers (a CountDownLatch of 1 that opens for everyone at once).
  2. Use more threads than cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, so the scheduler has to switch between them.
  3. Give each thread many operations, so the threads overlap for a long time.
  4. Run many rounds, with fresh state each time. One round is one sample of all the possible timings.
  5. When all the threads are done, check an invariant, a fact that must hold whatever the timing: totals that must add up, an amount that must never be passed. Never assert on how long something took.

The lab packs these habits into a small harness, a reusable piece of test code, called Stress. You give it a setup that builds fresh state, an actor that every thread runs over and over, and an invariant to check after join(). The figure shows one round. Here's the refund desk from the opening, under stress:

Java
record Round(RefundLedger ledger, AtomicLong approved) {}

int failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000,
        () -> new Round(new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)), new AtomicLong()),   // fresh state per round
        r -> { if (r.ledger().refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved().incrementAndGet(); },      // every thread, over and over
        r -> r.approved().get() == 10_000 && r.ledger().refunded("pay-1") == 10_000);     // must hold at the end
assertThat(failed).isZero();
Kotlin
class Round(val ledger: RefundLedger, val approved: AtomicLong)

val failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000,
    { Round(RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)), AtomicLong()) },              // fresh state per round
    { r -> if (r.ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved.incrementAndGet() },        // every thread, over and over
    { r -> r.approved.get() == 10_000L && r.ledger.refunded("pay-1") == 10_000L }) // must hold at the end
assertThat(failed).isZero()

Eight threads each try 2,000 one-cent refunds against a sale of 10,000 cents, so a correct ledger, the record that tracks the refunds, approves exactly 10,000. The racy ledger in the lab, which checks the total and then writes it in two separate steps, approves all 16,000. That's the coat refunded 160.00 on a 100.00 sale.

Two more rules keep these tests from hurting you. Put a timeout on every one, with @Timeout or assertTimeoutPreemptively from JUnit, the test library the labs use. Then a deadlock fails the test in seconds instead of hanging the whole test run for an hour. And remember what a pass means: this run found no failure. A stress test can prove that a race exists. It can never prove that none does, which is why the design rules from earlier lessons matter more than any test.

A passing race test means "not found this time", never "can't happen".

A stress test makes threads meet. The next trouble is a test that waits for its threads and guesses how long.

try.title: The same bug, tested two ways
steps: Read NaiveVsStress. It tests the racy counter from Race conditions twenty times the usual way (2 threads, 1,000 hits, no start line), then twenty times as a stress test (8 threads, 100,000 hits, a start latch).
Predict how many runs of each fail.
Run it two or three times.

code.title: NaiveVsStress.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. */ public class NaiveVsStress { static final class Counter { volatile int count; // volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) void hit() { count++; } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line static boolean naiveRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); return c.count == 2_000; } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together static boolean stressRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) c.hit(); }); ts[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return c.count == 800_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int naiveFailed = 0, stressFailed = 0; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!naiveRound()) naiveFailed++; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!stressRound()) stressFailed++; System.out.println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed " + naiveFailed + " of 20 runs"); System.out.println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed " + stressFailed + " of 20 runs"); } }

alt.title: NaiveVsStress.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. private class RacyCounter { @Volatile var count = 0 // @Volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) fun hit() { count++ } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line private fun naiveRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } a.join(); b.join() return c.count == 2_000 } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together private fun stressRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(100_000) { c.hit() } } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return c.count == 800_000 } fun main() { val naiveFailed = (1..20).count { !naiveRound() } val stressFailed = (1..20).count { !stressRound() } println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed $naiveFailed of 20 runs") println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed $stressFailed of 20 runs") }

try.expect: The naive test fails rarely, 0 or 1 of 20 in runs here, and a different number each time. The stress test fails 20 of 20. Same code, same bug. Only the second test is worth keeping.

video.title: Two test threads that never overlap catch nothing: a start latch, more threads than cores and many rounds make them collide, a latch with a deadline replaces the sleep, and jcstress counts every outcome

sections.h: Replacing sleeps with latches, and guesses with deadlines
sections.html:
Work that happens in the background, such as recording a refund after the customer has left the desk, is hard to test. The test has to wait until the work is done, and the quickest way to wait is a nap:

Java
// Naive: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them
worker.submit(refund);
Thread.sleep(50);
assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id())).isEqualTo(RECORDED);
Kotlin
// Naive: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them
worker.submit(refund)
Thread.sleep(50)
assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id)).isEqualTo(RECORDED)

Thread.sleep in a test is a guess about how long something takes. On your laptop the guess is generous, so the test is slow. On a busy build server, a shared machine that runs everyone's tests, the guess is too short, and the test fails for no reason. A test like that, which passes or fails with no change to the code, is called flaky, and a flaky test teaches the whole team to ignore red builds.

The Try it shows how quickly a guess goes wrong. Eight threads keep every core busy, like a build server on a busy afternoon. A background worker records a refund in about 2 ms. One test sleeps 3 ms and then checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times:

sleep(3) then assert:  failed 45 of 100
latch.await(5 s):      failed 0 of 100

A nap 50% longer than the work failed almost half the time. Another run here failed 14 of 100; on a busy machine, a guess is a coin toss. The fix is to wait for the event itself, and to keep the timeout only as a deadline far above any real duration:

Java
// Fixed: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration
CountDownLatch recorded = new CountDownLatch(1);
ledger.onRecorded(id -> recorded.countDown());
worker.submit(refund);
assertThat(recorded.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue();
assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id())).isEqualTo(RECORDED);
Kotlin
// Fixed: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration
val recorded = CountDownLatch(1)
ledger.onRecorded { recorded.countDown() }
worker.submit(refund)
assertThat(recorded.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue()
assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id)).isEqualTo(RECORDED)

The latch version is as fast as the code when the code is fast, and patient when the machine is slow. When it does fail, it fails with a clear message, "not recorded within 10 s", instead of a wrong status.

The same tools can hold a thread at a known point, which makes many concurrency tests deterministic: they give the same result on every run. Give the code under test a fake dependency that blocks on a latch, for example a fake bank service:

Java
class SlowBank implements Bank {
    final CountDownLatch inCall = new CountDownLatch(1);
    final CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);

    @Override
    public Approval check(Payment p) throws InterruptedException {
        inCall.countDown();          // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call
        release.await();             // 2. hold it here until the test says go
        return Approval.YES;
    }
}
Kotlin
class SlowBank : Bank {
    val inCall = CountDownLatch(1)
    val release = CountDownLatch(1)

    override fun check(p: Payment): Approval {
        inCall.countDown()           // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call
        release.await()              // 2. hold it here until the test says go
        return Approval.YES
    }
}

Now the test can wait on inCall and know for certain that one thread is inside the call. Plug this fake behind the IssuerGate from Synchronizers, the semaphore that guards the bank's card service, set to one permit. A second caller with a 100 ms limit must then time out. Finally the test opens release and checks that the permit came back. No sleeps, and no luck.

When there's no hook to wait on, poll: check the condition, sleep a few milliseconds, and check again, until an overall deadline passes. Checking Thread.getState() until the threads you expect are BLOCKED or WAITING is a common way to know they have queued up, and the worked example uses it.

A sleep in a test is a guess. Wait for the event, and keep the timeout as a deadline.

Latches and stress tests find the races you can provoke on purpose. Some bugs need millions of tries, and a tool built for exactly that.

try.title: Make a test flaky on purpose
steps: Read SleepVsLatch. Eight threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. A background worker records a refund in about 2 ms.
One test sleeps 3 ms and then checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times. Predict the failure counts.
Run it. Then change the sleep to 10 ms and run it again.

code.title: SleepVsLatch.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A test checks that a background worker records a refund. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; * the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. */ public class SleepVsLatch { static volatile boolean burn = true; // the code under test: records the refund on another thread, about 2 ms of work static Thread recordAsync(Runnable whenDone) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { long end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); whenDone.run(); }); t.start(); return t; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread b = new Thread(() -> { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait(); }); // a busy machine b.setDaemon(true); b.start(); } int sleepFailed = 0, latchFailed = 0; for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { boolean[] recorded = {false}; Thread t = recordAsync(() -> recorded[0] = true); Thread.sleep(3); // "should be enough" if (!recorded[0]) sleepFailed++; // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join(); } for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { CountDownLatch recorded = new CountDownLatch(1); recordAsync(recorded::countDown); if (!recorded.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++; // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false; System.out.println("sleep(3) then assert: failed " + sleepFailed + " of 100"); System.out.println("latch.await(5 s): failed " + latchFailed + " of 100"); } }

alt.title: SleepVsLatch.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A test checks that a background worker records a refund. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; // the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. @Volatile private var burn = true // the code under test: records the refund on another thread, about 2 ms of work private fun recordAsync(whenDone: () -> Unit): Thread = thread { val end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() whenDone() } fun main() { repeat(8) { thread(isDaemon = true) { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait() } } // a busy machine var sleepFailed = 0 var latchFailed = 0 repeat(100) { var recorded = false val t = recordAsync { recorded = true } Thread.sleep(3) // "should be enough" if (!recorded) sleepFailed++ // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join() } repeat(100) { val recorded = CountDownLatch(1) recordAsync { recorded.countDown() } if (!recorded.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++ // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false println("sleep(3) then assert: failed $sleepFailed of 100") println("latch.await(5 s): failed $latchFailed of 100") }

try.expect: The sleep version failed 14 and 45 times out of 100 in two runs here. The latch version failed 0 times. A 10 ms sleep fails less often, but it can still fail, and it makes every run slower.

sections.h: Letting jcstress search the timings for you
sections.html:
Some bugs need millions of attempts to show up at all, and some need a particular kind of processor. ARM processors, such as the ones in Apple Silicon laptops and many cloud servers, may let one core see another core's writes in a different order from how they were made. Intel and AMD processors allow less of that. jcstress is a harness for exactly these bugs, from OpenJDK, the open-source project that builds Java itself. It runs tiny tests millions of times, with careful control over how the threads start and where the state lives, and it counts every outcome it sees. Its latest tagged release is 0.16, from February 2023, and the master branch is 0.17-SNAPSHOT.

A jcstress test is a class with shared @State, two or more @Actor methods that run at the same time, and a result object, here II_Result, which holds two int fields. @Outcome annotations list the results you expect and label each one. Here's the race from the first section, as two refund desks bumping one counter:

import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*;
import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.II_Result;
import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*;

@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "1, 2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor1 went first")
@Outcome(id = "2, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor2 went first")
@Outcome(id = "1, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING, desc = "both read 0: one increment lost")
@State
public class RefundCounterRace {
    int refunds;                                  // shared state, fresh for every sample

    @Actor
    public void actor1(II_Result r) { r.r1 = ++refunds; }

    @Actor
    public void actor2(II_Result r) { r.r2 = ++refunds; }
}

jcstress is a Java-only tool. An annotation processor, a plug-in that runs inside the compiler, turns these classes into test code at build time, so there's no Kotlin twin here.

The labels are the part to learn:

  • ACCEPTABLE is a correct result.
  • ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING is allowed but worth seeing, usually the race the test is about. Here, 1, 1 means both actors read 0, so one increment was lost.
  • FORBIDDEN must never happen. If jcstress sees it even once, the test fails.

Write down your guess: how often will 1, 1 happen? Here's a real run, on a 4-core x86 Linux machine with JDK 21. It took under two minutes:

  RESULT      SAMPLES     FREQ       EXPECT  DESCRIPTION
    1, 1  707,991,481   36.34%  Interesting  both read 0: one increment lost
    1, 2  675,088,320   34.65%   Acceptable  actor1 went first
    2, 1  565,287,693   29.01%   Acceptable  actor2 went first

Almost two billion samples, and the increment was lost in more than a third of them. That's the same bug the naive test caught once in twenty runs. jcstress doesn't hope the threads meet; it arranges for them to meet, two billion times. With an AtomicInteger instead of the plain int, a rerun on the same machine never saw 1, 1 at all, and jcstress listed no interesting results. Had we marked 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test would have failed.

Results depend on the hardware. x86 processors, the Intel and AMD kind, keep their writes in order, so some surprises that ARM machines show regularly, such as one thread seeing another's writes out of order, may never appear on an Intel laptop. Interesting means allowed, not guaranteed to appear. The README documents a Maven project template and no official Gradle setup, so try it in a separate Maven project. (Maven is a Java build tool, like the Gradle that runs this course's labs.) The jcstress samples on GitHub are a course in themselves. Each one has the outcomes it expects written in its source.

Tests find bugs before a program ships. When a running program misbehaves anyway, you need the JVM to tell you what its threads are doing.

steps: In a scratch folder outside the labs, make a jcstress project with the template command below, from the jcstress README. Maven downloads what it needs the first time.
Add RefundCounterRace from this section to the generated sources, build, and run only that test with -t. A run takes a minute or two and keeps every core busy.
Find the line for outcome 1, 1. Then change int refunds to an AtomicInteger and both actors to incrementAndGet(), rebuild and run again.

code.html: mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress \ -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 cd test # put RefundCounterRace.java next to the generated sample test, then: mvn clean verify java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t RefundCounterRace

With AtomicInteger, 1, 1 is never seen, and the run lists no interesting tests. If you mark 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test fails.

sections.h: When it hangs, take dumps; when it's slow, record JFR
sections.html:
Once a program runs for real, you debug it with what the JVM can tell you about itself. Two tools cover most cases, and both come with the JDK, the kit you install to build and run Java.

A thread dump answers "where is every thread right now, and what is it waiting for?". It's a printout of every thread's name, state and stack, the chain of method calls the thread is in the middle of. jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l prints one: jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and the PID is the number the operating system gives each running program. The -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns, and the dump ends with a deadlock report if there's a cycle (Deadlock, livelock and starvation). The state line is the first thing to read:

What the dump says What the thread is doing
RUNNABLE Running, ready to run, or waiting inside the operating system for input, such as data from the network
BLOCKED (on object monitor) Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds
WAITING (parking) Parked by java.util.concurrent: a lock, latch, queue or semaphore; the parking to wait for line names it
WAITING (on object monitor) Inside Object.wait()
TIMED_WAITING The same, with a timeout, or in sleep

Here's a trimmed dump of a small program in which till-0 takes a ReentrantLock and then makes a slow call while holding it, and three other tills wait for the lock. It was taken on JDK 25:

"till-0" #23 [14677] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.24ms elapsed=2.54s ...
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
	at java.lang.Thread.sleep(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:540)
	at Stuck.slowCall(Stuck.java:17)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x000000073781f198> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)

"till-1" #24 [14678] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.59ms elapsed=2.34s ...
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x000000073781f198> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)
	...
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock.lock(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ReentrantLock.java:323)
	at Stuck.lambda$main$1(Stuck.java:12)

Read it from the waiting side. till-1 is parked, waiting for the lock at ...f198. The same address appears under till-0's "Locked ownable synchronizers", so till-0 holds it, and its stack says why it's slow: it's asleep in slowCall, still holding the lock. That's the rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks, keep slow calls out of the lock, broken in a real program.

One dump is a photo. Take three, a few seconds apart: a thread that shows the same frame every time is stuck, and one whose stack changes is busy. In this program's third dump, four seconds later, till-1 still showed cpu=0.59ms, while elapsed had grown from 2.34 s to 6.58 s. That's a thread that exists, waits and does nothing. For tools of your own, Thread.dump_to_file -format=json writes the same dump as JSON, with state and lock fields from JDK 25.

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) answers a different question: "what were the threads waiting for over the last minute, and for how long?". It's an event recorder built into the JVM, cheap enough to leave on in production. jdk.JavaMonitorEnter records each wait to enter a synchronized block that lasts longer than a threshold, with the lock's class, the duration and the previous owner. jdk.JavaMonitorWait covers Object.wait(), and jdk.ThreadPark covers ReentrantLock and the other java.util.concurrent waits.

jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l                          # states, stacks, owned j.u.c locks, deadlocks
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json t.json  # JSON; per-thread state and lock fields need JDK 25+
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=locks.jfr
jfr summary locks.jfr                               # how many events of each type
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter locks.jfr   # who waited for which monitor, how long, after whom

The Try it records one second of six threads fighting, three over a synchronized block and three over a ReentrantLock, each holding its lock for 3 ms at a time. I expected hundreds of short waits for both. The ReentrantLock gave exactly that. The monitor, in most runs here on JDK 21 and JDK 25, gave something else. Here's one run on JDK 25:

JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object                                       3 events,   1975 ms waiting
ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync       326 events,   1728 ms waiting

Three waits for the monitor, adding up to almost two seconds. jfr print on the same recording shows one of the two long ones:

jdk.JavaMonitorEnter {
  startTime = 17:45:51.586 (2026-11-16)
  duration = 986 ms
  monitorClass = java.lang.Object (classLoader = bootstrap)
  previousOwner = "ledger-2" (javaThreadId = 28)
  address = 0x7FB344000F20
  eventThread = "ledger-4" (javaThreadId = 30)
  ...
}

ledger-4 waited 986 ms to get in, and the thread that held the monitor just before it was ledger-2. In other words, ledger-2 released the monitor and took it straight back, over and over, while the other two threads waited for nearly the whole second. synchronized makes no promise of fairness, and here one thread kept the lock for almost a second: the starvation from Deadlock, livelock and starvation, now with numbers. (One busy run here split the waiting into 94 shorter events instead, so take a few recordings before you decide.) A single thread dump would have shown two BLOCKED threads and nothing more. The recording showed who waited, how long, and for whom.

No JFR event reports deadlocks; for those, use a dump or ThreadMXBean, the JDK's window onto the JVM's threads. And if your program runs in a container, a packaged and walled-off environment that many servers use, the JVM is often process 1, so jcmd 1 Thread.print inside the container is the quickest start.

try.title: Record contention with JFR
steps: Read JfrContention. It starts a JFR recording from inside the program, runs six threads for one second (three fight over a synchronized block, three over a ReentrantLock), then reads the recording back.
Predict the number of events and the total waiting time for each kind of lock. Then run it.
Run jfr summary and then jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter on the file the demo printed. Find duration and previousOwner.

code.title: JfrContention.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; /** * Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, * then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. */ public class JfrContention { static final Object ledgerMonitor = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock batchLock = new ReentrantLock(); static void busy(long micros) { long end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start(); long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; Thread[] ts = new Thread[6]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { boolean useMonitor = i % 2 == 0; ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) { synchronized (ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000); } // hold it 3 ms } else { batchLock.lock(); try { busy(3_000); } finally { batchLock.unlock(); } } } }, (useMonitor ? "ledger-" : "batch-") + i); ts[i].start(); } for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); } Map<String, long[]> byKind = new TreeMap<>(); // count, total ms for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { String what = switch (e.getEventType().getName()) { case "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").getName(); case "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass") == null ? "?" : e.getClass("parkedClass").getName()); default -> e.getEventType().getName(); }; long[] agg = byKind.computeIfAbsent(what, k -> new long[2]); agg[0]++; agg[1] += e.getDuration().toMillis(); } byKind.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.printf("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting%n", k, v[0], v[1])); System.out.println("recording kept at " + file); } }

alt.title: JfrContention.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.nio.file.Files import java.time.Duration import java.util.TreeMap import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import jdk.jfr.Recording import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, // then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. private val ledgerMonitor = Any() private val batchLock = ReentrantLock() private fun busy(micros: Long) { val end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() } fun main() { val file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr") Recording().use { rec -> rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start() val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L val ts = List(6) { i -> val useMonitor = i % 2 == 0 thread(name = (if (useMonitor) "ledger-" else "batch-") + i) { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) synchronized(ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000) } // hold it 3 ms else batchLock.withLock { busy(3_000) } } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } rec.stop() rec.dump(file) } val byKind = TreeMap<String, LongArray>() // count, total ms for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { val what = when (e.eventType.name) { "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").name "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass")?.name ?: "?") else -> e.eventType.name } val agg = byKind.getOrPut(what) { LongArray(2) } agg[0]++ agg[1] += e.duration.toMillis() } byKind.forEach { (k, v) -> println("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting".format(k, v[0], v[1])) } println("recording kept at $file") }

try.expect: ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync with about 320 events and about 1.7 seconds of waiting in total. JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object with only a handful of events (2 to 8 in most runs here), adding up to almost two seconds: one thread kept taking the monitor back while two others waited. A busy machine can split the waiting into many shorter events. jfr print shows each event's duration, monitorClass, previousOwner and the waiting thread's stack.

compare.title: The same stress test in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java (JUnit 6)
java.html: @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build void noRefundIsLost() throws Exception { RefundLedger ledger = new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)); AtomicLong approved = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { // more threads than cores Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); // the starting gun for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000); // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin (JUnit 6)
kotlin.html: @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build fun `no refund is lost`() { val ledger = RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)) val approved = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { // more threads than cores thread { go.await() repeat(2_000) { if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet() } } } go.countDown() // the starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000L) // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000L) }

compare.note: JUnit, AssertJ and the latches work the same from both languages, and the Java version is already short for what it does. Kotlin trims the ceremony: thread { } starts a thread in one line, List(8) { ... } collects them, and with no checked exceptions there's no try and catch around go.await(). Two details differ. Backtick test names read like specs. And AssertJ needs 10_000L in Kotlin: assertThat(aLong).isEqualTo(10_000) would pass an Int, which picks the Object overload and fails, because a Long 10,000 isn't equal to an Integer 10,000. For coroutine code, Kotlin has a tool Java lacks: kotlinx-coroutines-test runs suspending code on virtual time, so tests of delays and timeouts run instantly and give the same result every run. The coroutines track covers it.

worked.title: Turn a flaky "loads once" test into a deterministic one

steps.say: A cache keeps each answer from a slow web service, so the service is asked only once, like the caches in Concurrent collections. This test is meant to prove that PriceCache loads the price of bread once when eight callers ask together. Read it and decide what it actually tests.
steps.code: // Naive: tests the scheduler, not the cache @Test void loadsOnce() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); PriceCache cache = new PriceCache(item -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return 250L; }); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) new Thread(() -> cache.priceOf("bread")).start(); Thread.sleep(100); // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); }

alt.html: // Naive: tests the scheduler, not the cache @Test fun `loads once`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val cache = PriceCache { loads.incrementAndGet(); 250L } repeat(8) { thread { cache.priceOf("bread") } } Thread.sleep(100) // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) }

steps.say: It tests the scheduler. The loader is so fast that the threads rarely overlap, so a racy cache that checks with get and then stores with put passes too. And on a slow machine the threads might not have run at all within 100 ms, so loads is 0 and a correct cache fails. The fix is to control the timing: hold the first load inside the loader until every caller is known to be waiting, then let it go.
Here's the deterministic version, with a label on each step. The loader blocks on a latch, and the test polls the thread states, with a deadline, until all eight callers are waiting.
steps.code: @Test @Timeout(10) void loadsOnceWhileOthersWait() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch inLoader = new CountDownLatch(1), release = new CountDownLatch(1); PriceCache cache = new PriceCache(item -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); inLoader.countDown(); // 1. a caller is inside the loader try { release.await(); } // and stays there until we say go catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 250L; }); List<Thread> callers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> cache.priceOf("bread")); t.start(); callers.add(t); } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); awaitParked(callers, 8); // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown(); // 3. let the load finish for (Thread t : callers) t.join(); assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); // 4. one load served all eight } static void awaitParked(List<Thread> threads, int n) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5); while (threads.stream().filter(t -> t.getState() == Thread.State.BLOCKED || t.getState() == Thread.State.WAITING).count() < n) { if (System.nanoTime() > deadline) throw new AssertionError("callers never queued up"); Thread.sleep(5); // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } }

alt.html: @Test @Timeout(10) fun `loads once while others wait`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val inLoader = CountDownLatch(1) val release = CountDownLatch(1) val cache = PriceCache { loads.incrementAndGet() inLoader.countDown() // 1. a caller is inside the loader release.await() // and stays there until we say go 250L } val callers = List(8) { thread { cache.priceOf("bread") } } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue() awaitParked(callers, 8) // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown() // 3. let the load finish callers.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) // 4. one load served all eight } fun awaitParked(threads: List<Thread>, n: Int) { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5) while (threads.count { it.state == Thread.State.BLOCKED || it.state == Thread.State.WAITING } < n) { check(System.nanoTime() < deadline) { "callers never queued up" } Thread.sleep(5) // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself why this version fails on the racy cache every time. Answer: with get-then-put, every caller misses and enters the loader, so all eight end up waiting on release inside it, and step 2 is satisfied. When the test opens the latch, all eight loads finish, and loads is 8. With computeIfAbsent, one caller is inside the loader and the other seven are BLOCKED on the part of the map that holds that key, so loads is 1. The result no longer depends on luck, only on the code.

lab.title: A stress harness that catches races, and a refund race to fix
steps: Meet the two classes. Stress is the harness from the first section, and you'll write it. RefundLedger is the refund desk: refund(paymentId, cents) pays back part of a payment if the total stays within what was actually paid (the code calls that the captured amount), and returns whether it did.
Run the tests. Six of the seven fail. The five Stress tests hit UnsupportedOperationException, and the ledger's load test approves 16,000 one-cent refunds against 10,000 cents paid.

Write Stress.failingRounds. For each round: call setup, create a ready latch and a go latch, and start threads threads that count down ready, wait on go, then run the actor perThread times. Wait on ready, count down go, join every thread, then test the invariant and count the failures.
Run the tests again. The Stress tests should pass, including the two that point your harness at racy code (a volatile counter and a check-then-act ledger) and expect it to find failures.
Fix RefundLedger.refund: do the check and the update inside one refunded.compute(...) call, and call writeAuditLine() after it, only when the refund was approved.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more.
hints: The start line is the Hammer from Race conditions. Make the actor threads daemons, so a stuck actor can't keep the JVM alive.
The join() does two jobs: it waits, and it makes everything the actors wrote visible to the thread that checks the invariant.
Inside compute, return already unchanged (it may be null) to reject a refund. Record the decision in a local boolean[1] or an AtomicBoolean, because a lambda can't assign a local variable.
lab.done: All seven tests in ConcurrencyTestingTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A stress test from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a JUnit test that checks a Counter (with increment() and total()) loses nothing when 8 threads each call increment() 50,000 times. Then check: do the threads start together, does a deadlock fail the test, and is your assertion an invariant rather than a timing?

answer.html: @Test @Timeout(10) void countsEveryIncrement() throws Exception { Counter counter = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) counter.increment(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(counter.total()).isEqualTo(8 * 50_000); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: @Test @Timeout(10) fun `counts every increment from 8 threads`() { val counter = Counter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(50_000) { counter.increment() } } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(counter.total()).isEqualTo(8 * 50_000) }

recap: A stress test forces overlap: a start latch, more threads than cores, many operations, many rounds with fresh state, and an invariant checked after join().
Every concurrency test gets a timeout. A pass means "not found this time", never "can't happen".
Replace Thread.sleep in tests with latches or polling with a deadline. A fake that blocks on a latch holds a thread at a known point.
jcstress runs tiny tests millions of times and labels each outcome ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING or FORBIDDEN; a forbidden outcome seen even once fails the test.
Thread dumps show where every thread is and what it waits for; take several, seconds apart. JFR's JavaMonitorEnter and ThreadPark events show who waited, for how long, and after whom.
The limit: tests and tools find the bugs that happen. Only the design rules of this track keep them from being possible.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "Our concurrency test has been green for months, so the class is thread-safe." Explain what a green stress test does and doesn't tell you, and what you'd check about the test itself.
explain.answer: A green run means the test didn't happen to hit a bad timing, not that no bad timing exists. Races depend on timing, hardware and load, so a test can stay green for months and the race can still fire on a busy day. I'd check that the test really makes threads collide. It needs a start latch, more threads than cores, enough operations per thread, many rounds with fresh state, and an assertion on an invariant rather than on timing. I'd check that it has a timeout, so a deadlock would fail it. And I'd still review the class against the rules of this track: what state is shared, which lock or atomic protects each compound action, and whether anything calls out while holding a lock. Tests find races; design prevents them.

deeper.html:
jcstress has more than actors and outcomes. An @Arbiter method runs after all actors have finished and can record the final state into the result, which suits tests like "after two increments, is the counter 2?". Termination tests, marked @JCStressTest(Mode.Termination) with a @Signal method, check whether a thread ever notices a signal; the sample BasicJMM_04_Progress uses this to show whether a spin loop ever sees a field change. The runner has modes too: the README mentions -m quick, which many build servers use to keep runs short.

For Kotlin code, JetBrains' Lincheck library tests concurrent data structures by running operations from several threads, including in a model-checking mode that explores the possible timings one by one. Then it checks that the results match some one-at-a-time order of the same operations. It's worth a look before you write a lock-free structure.

JFR is not only a file format. jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, added in JDK 14 (JEP 349), streams events to your code while the program runs. A service can subscribe to jdk.JavaMonitorEnter and report a number when waits on one class go over a budget.

Finally, the JDK's own tools can be scripted. jcmd <pid> help lists every diagnostic command a JVM supports, and the list changes between versions: JDK 24 added Thread.vthread_scheduler and Thread.vthread_pollers for virtual threads, and from JDK 24 Thread.print also includes virtual threads that are mounted on a carrier. The virtual threads track uses those.
